chapters.title: Cancellation curves
chapters.subtitle: why Euler's line of primes stops where it does

lines.text: Every composite number is a product: u times u plus d. Fix the gap d, let u run, and the products line up on one curve of the spiral. These are the cancellation curves.
Each curve is born at the number d plus one, the little ring, and everything after its birth is composite. A prime sits on exactly one curve: the one born at it.
Gap zero is the squares, gap one the pronic numbers. On the saddle every one of these curves climbs the ridge, because a product of two nearly equal numbers lands near the x axis.

Flatten the saddle and follow Euler's line, k squared plus k plus forty-one, past its forty primes. Wherever it meets a cancellation curve the value is composite, and the meetings come in two families.
Family one: at k equal to forty plus a square, the value is the product of two neighbouring values of the line itself. Forty-one times forty-three, forty-three times forty-seven, and on it goes.

Family two reaches in from a sister line, four j squared plus one hundred and sixty-three: a value of the sister times a value of Euler. Both families are products in one quadratic ring, the ring of root minus one sixty-three, and that is all the arithmetic there is.
Now ask the zeros instead. The master wave of all ten thousand zeros, evaluated along the line, spikes at every prime value and dips at every crossing. The zeros and the curves agree point by point.

chapters.title: Level contours
chapters.subtitle: slicing the saddle at a height

lines.text: The saddle is z equals x squared minus y squared, scaled down. Slice it with a horizontal plane and the cut is a hyperbola: opening left and right above the middle, up and down below it.

Here are the cuts at heights fifteen and thirty on the ridge side, opening along the squares and pronic rays. Every number lit on one contour shares the same value of n times the cosine of four pi root n.
Below the middle, on the valley side, the contours open along the y axis instead. The valley is where the one-to-four products live: u times four u plus an odd number.
Seen from the side the planes are real cuts through the surface. The valley planes also cut the trail of zeta rising from the centre: a plane at minus h meets the trail at the dial value four h.
At height zero the hyperbola collapses into the two diagonals, and a third family hugs them: the one-to-sixteen products. Each direction of the saddle collects its own family of products.

And the quantity shared along every contour, n cosine four pi root n, is the first harmonic of Voronoi's formula for the divisor function. The saddle is not decoration: its level lines are the contour lines of the divisor wave.

chapters.title: The bend as a probe
chapters.subtitle: a fixed plane sweeps the curves as the saddle bends

lines.text: Start flat. The ridge family in orange, the valley family in blue, the diagonal family in white, all drawn on a flat spiral. A plane at height fifteen touches nothing yet.
Bend the saddle a quarter of the way. The plane at minus fifteen now cuts the valley near the rim, around n equals thirteen hundred and seventy, and lights every number it crosses.
Half the bend, and the contour has moved inward to n near six hundred and eighty. The valley curves dive faster now, so the plane reads them off closer to the centre.
The tour's own bend, one. The contour sits at n three hundred and forty, and each blue curve crosses it in exactly one place: the plane is reading the curves like the teeth of a comb.

Bend it twice as hard and the contour closes in to n near one hundred and seventy. Nothing on the vertical planes has moved: the ridge still holds the squares and the pronics, the valley still holds the one-to-four products.
So the bend is a probe, not a parameter of the arithmetic. It decides which contour a plane picks, never which numbers sit on which curve. Sweeping it maps where every curve crosses that height.
Back to the tour's saddle. What the plane found on the way is the geometry of the curves themselves: where each family climbs, dives, or stays level.

chapters.title: Mirrors, not oracles
chapters.subtitle: the vortices of the chain at a zero

lines.text: This is the chain at the hundred and fifty-ninth zero: every link one term of the series, curling into vortices before it settles. Let's find their eyes with nothing but the turning angles.
Where the turn between links flips through a half-turn, the chain folds back on itself. That knot is an eye. Where the turn flips through zero the chain runs straight: a spoke, the edge of a vortex.

A vortex drawn by dozens of links is certain; one drawn by two or three is a guess, so its ring is faded. Now the crosses: the chain's own first vertices, reflected and turned by twice the Gram phase.
They land inside the rings. At the thousandth zero, with far more links, every eye out to the twelfth sits on its mirror to a thousandth. The far end of the chain is its near end in a mirror.
Stack the zeros as planes and trace each eye through them. Vortex one, in cyan, winds once around the axis per zero on a circle of radius exactly one. Vortex two rides an epicycle on it.
Take the Gram phase out and the whole tower collapses: vortex one to a single point, vortex two to a circle, vortex three to an epicycle. These are the chain's first terms, nothing more.
All ten thousand zeros seen down the axis: the unit circle of vortex one, the rings of the rest. This is as much structure as there is.

With the phase removed: the point, the circle, the epicycles. The eye angle at a zero reads that zero's Gram offset. It correlates with the next gap at minus a quarter, and with the next zero's offset not at all.
So each vortex is a mirror of the zero it sits at: the chain's own beginning, reflected through that zero's phase. It is not an oracle for the zero to come. Mirrors, not oracles.

Count the whole-number points under the curve u times v equals x. Each one is a factor pair, a point on a cancellation curve. The count grows like x log x, and the white line is how it wobbles around that. Each faint line marks one turn of the spiral.
Voronoi wrote that wobble as a sum of waves, one cosine of four pi root n x for each n. Here they arrive one by one, and the cyan sum settles onto the white.
The first wave on its own goes up and down twice on every turn of the spiral. That is the saddle itself. The surface the tour is drawn on is the first wave of the divisor problem.
Now count the points inside a circle of radius root x instead. There are about pi x of them, and this count wobbles too.
Hardy found its waves: two pi root n x, weighted by the number of ways to write n as a sum of two squares. They run half as fast, one up and down per turn. Watch them add up.

A wave that rises once per turn needs a different surface. Twist the saddle by half a turn for every turn of the spiral. The squares slide onto the crests and fall away, the pronic numbers slide into the troughs and rise, and the orange wave slows from two crests per turn to one.

So the two counting problems have two surfaces. The divisor wobble, made of the points on the cancellation curves, rides on two waves per turn: the saddle. The circle wobble, made of the points on the mirror lines, rides on one wave per turn: the saddle's half-twist.
Both wobbles are believed to grow no faster than about the fourth root of x. For neither problem has anyone proved it.

Euler's k squared plus k plus forty-one measures the size of numbers in a ring built on the square root of minus one hundred sixty-three. In that ring some ordinary primes break into two pieces. They split. The others stay whole.

Only a prime that splits can divide one of Euler's numbers, and the first prime that splits is forty-one. That is why his first forty values are all prime. Gold marks the primes that split, blue the primes that stay whole.

The zeros of zeta build a wave that rises at every prime, by the explicit formula. Here they arrive, all five and a half thousand below height six thousand. Every prime gets the same needle, every prime square half of one.

Now a second set of zeros: the zeros of the L-function of minus one sixty-three, ten thousand four hundred and sixty-two of them below the same height, computed for this. As they join, the needles at the blue primes sink away and the gold ones double.
Below forty-one nothing is left standing except four, nine, sixteen and twenty-five: squares of primes that stay whole, which are the sizes of those primes inside the ring.
Together the two sets of zeros count the primes of Euler's ring. Every composite value of his polynomial, every crossing of a cancellation curve with his line, is built from the gold spikes.
The extra zeros say which primes can divide Euler's numbers, which is what one Legendre symbol already says. They do not say which of his values are prime.

chapters.title: Mirror lines
chapters.subtitle: one pair proves a prime, two pairs factor

lines.text: On the squares side of the spiral the cancellation curves are k squared minus m squared. Every value is a difference of two squares, so every value factors.
Reflect them across the squares ray and the minus becomes a plus. They swing over into k squared plus m squared: sums of two squares.
Through every number pass some pairs of these mirror lines, one pair for each way to write it as a sum of two squares. Gold numbers have exactly one pair. Red numbers have two or more.
One pair proves a prime. Sixteen oh one is forty squared plus one squared, and no other pair of squares. So it is prime. This is Euler's criterion.

Two pairs prove a composite, and hand over a factor. Two twenty-one is fourteen squared plus five squared and also eleven squared plus ten squared. One greatest common divisor turns those into seventeen.
Eleven oh five sits on four pairs, and its factors fall out the same way: thirteen, five and seventeen.

Fermat works the other side of the mirror. He walks out along the squares until m squared minus n is itself a square. For fifteen oh one that takes ten steps, and the curve he finds is the cancellation curve through it.
Euler's test works only for his sixty-five idoneal numbers, and both methods are slower than modern tests. What the spiral adds is the picture: one search on each side of the mirror.
Every curve on the spiral is a quadratic. Far from the centre it straightens into a line, and its distance from its ray is set by one number, its discriminant.
Slide a vertical plane across the squares side and it picks up one quadratic at a time. Red when the quadratic factors. Blue or green when it does not.
Count the primes on every plane, for k up to three thousand. Only the planes whose quadratic factors come up empty.
The white ticks are the Hardy–Littlewood predictions, from the discriminant alone. They match the counts with a correlation of 0.9995.

On the pronic side, Euler's k squared plus k plus forty-one is the record, at discriminant minus one sixty-three. And a line among the cancellation curves, k squared plus k minus one, beats Landau's k squared plus one.

Two of these curves meet only where the difference of their discriminants factors. Euler's line and k squared plus one meet at exactly two numbers, one ninety-seven and sixteen oh one, and both are prime.

chapters.title: Pinching the spiral
chapters.subtitle: four ways to pile up the primes

lines.text: A pinch brings far-apart parts of the spiral together, so whatever they share piles up in one place. First, the fold: double every angle, and the squares ray and the pronic ray fall onto one ray.
Now every quadratic straightens at a distance set by its discriminant alone, from both sides at once. The two half combs merge into one comb of every discriminant.

The prime two shows up as a stripe. Lines whose discriminant is five mod eight never take an even value, and they average four hundred and thirty-eight primes. The lines at one mod eight are always even.
The residue pinch slides every number around its own circle to the angle two pi n over m. The spiral collapses onto m arms, one for each remainder.

The primes ride only the arms that share no factor with m. Modulo thirty that is eight arms, each almost four times richer in primes. The rest are cancellation arms, and their only prime is the one dividing thirty.
Pinched modulo four on the saddle, the two prime arms are exactly its two rising lobes, and the even numbers fall away down the valleys.
The pleat folds each turn into thirty slots after the pronic ray, and slot j becomes the curve k squared plus k plus j.

The primes gather on two curves named by Euler's lucky numbers, k squared plus k plus eleven, and plus seventeen. The white marks are the composites the pleat cannot see, built from primes larger than five.
On the squares side a curve takes both odd and even values, so it can never dodge two. That is why the prime-rich Euler lines all live on the pronic side.
Pinch by three, five and seven at once, as three axes, and every odd number falls into one cell of a lattice. The primes fill exactly the forty-eight cells off the three zero planes.

Every pinch gathers primes the way the sieve does, and no better: the best curve is richer by the product of p over p minus one, for the primes it sees. Euler's line sees every prime up to thirty-seven. The pinch shows the sieve as geometry. It cannot beat it.

chapters.title: The 12 × 12 torus
chapters.subtitle: turn and step, counted in twelves

lines.text: Every number on the spiral has two coordinates. Its turn is the ring it sits on, and its step is how far round that ring it has come from the square that starts it. Forty-one is six squared plus five: turn six, step five.
Count turn and step in twelves, and every number lands on a twelve by twelve board. Here come the primes up to ten million, each dropped into its cell.

Above three, the primes land in only forty-eight of the hundred and forty-four cells: the cells where the number leaves remainder one, five, seven or eleven after division by twelve. Two and three are the only primes anywhere else.
On this board every curve of the spiral becomes a straight line. The curves k squared plus k plus c run diagonally. Follow c equal to five and eleven: every cell they cross is gold.
One and seven cross gold in eight rows out of twelve. Three and nine, in four. Even values of c never cross gold at all, so those lines carry no primes.

On average, a line's share of the primes is three times its share of gold rows: three for five and eleven, two for one and seven, one for three and nine, nothing for the rest. Euler's forty-one, seventeen and eleven all sit in the top class.

The vertical lines are the curves on the other side of the spiral, k squared plus C. None of them stays gold for more than half its rows, so none can beat one and a half. That is why the prime-rich lines all live on the pronic side.
Roll the board up, the step the short way round and the turn the long way, and it becomes a torus. The two gold diagonals close into loops that wind once around it both ways.
Back on the spiral, the gold lines are Euler's family. Everything the board shows comes from dividing by two and three. It cannot see a single prime beyond them.

Slide every number round its own ring to the angle of its remainder after division by twenty-four. The primes gather on eight arms. Each is coloured by one question: is three a perfect square modulo that prime? Cyan if it is, magenta if not.
Now raise the saddle. Every cyan prime falls away, and every magenta prime rises. The height of each prime is the Legendre symbol of three, computed by the shape of the surface.
There are no exceptions among the primes up to two million. The reason is a single identity: the cosine of thirty degrees is half the square root of three.
Sixteen arms do the same for two. Primes one or seven more than a multiple of eight fall away; primes three or five more rise.
Ten arms compute five, but at two unequal heights, about plus zero point three and minus zero point eight: the two halves of the square root of five.
A hundred and forty-four arms on a twelve-fold saddle give the same answer for three: the forty-eight prime arms rise or fall by exactly the same amount.
The saddle's height is a cosine, and for these moduli a cosine is a Legendre symbol in disguise. It says which primes have three, two or five as a square, and nothing about which numbers are prime.

chapters.title: Base-12 fingerprints
chapters.subtitle: the last two digits of a curve

lines.text: Write a number in base twelve and keep its last two digits. There are a hundred and forty-four possible endings: a twelve by twelve board, the dozens digit down the side and the units digit across.
Every prime above three ends in one, five, seven or b, the four columns that share no factor with twelve. Here are the primes up to a million, filling exactly those columns.
A curve leaves its own fingerprint. The squares, one value at a time, light only sixteen cells, and just six of them in the prime columns.
Euler's k squared plus k plus forty-one lights thirty-two cells, and every one of them is in a prime column. In base twelve its values end in five or b twice as often as in one or seven.
k squared plus k plus seventeen also stays inside the prime columns, through a different set of rows.
The pronic numbers never reach a prime column at all. A product of two neighbours is always even.
Side by side, the fingerprints show which remainders by two and three each curve avoids. That is all they can show: past three, the board is blind.

Far from the centre, every curve straightens into a line pointing in a direction set by its middle coefficient. The directions that are whole multiples of a twenty-fourth of a turn are the hours of a clock.
On every hour lies a product family, u times q squared u plus d, where q squared divides a hundred and forty-four: one, four, nine, sixteen, thirty-six or a hundred and forty-four.
Fourteen hours hold no primes at all near their rays: the twelve even hours, and hours three and twenty-one.
The other ten hold a few primes, carried by quadratics that sit just beside the product family, like sixteen k squared plus eleven k plus two at hour nine.
On the saddle, the hours bend with the surface, and each family climbs or falls along it.
The clock's numbers are the square divisors of a hundred and forty-four. Twelve times twelve is the natural size for the primes two and three, and nothing in it can see beyond them.

chapters.title: Mirrors for prime pairs
chapters.subtitle: the curves without primes reflect the most

lines.text: Every number is a mirror. Step the same distance to either side of a number on the pronic ray, and the two numbers you land on sit symmetric across the ray.

When both are prime, they are a Goldbach pair: two primes that add up to twice the mirror, joined by a chord across the ray. Across thirty turns, from turn ten on, the pronic mirrors reflect fifty-four pairs.

Now Euler's line, k squared plus k plus forty-one, the most prime-rich curve on the spiral. Over the same thirty turns its mirrors reflect only sixteen pairs, and half of its mirrors reflect none at all.

Over two thousand turns the gap holds. The pronic mirrors reflect two point one five times as many prime pairs as Euler's, the squares one and a half times as many, and Euler's line is the weakest mirror of all.

The white ticks are a prediction, not a measurement. Hardy and Littlewood's form of Goldbach's conjecture multiplies a mirror's pairs by p minus one over p minus two for every odd prime p that divides it. The ticks land on the bars.

The reason is simple. When p divides the mirror, p can spoil a pair only when it also divides the step: one way instead of two. Pronic numbers are always even, and two times in three divisible by three. Euler's values have no prime factor below forty-one.
A chord is an unordered pair of angles, and the unordered pairs of points on a circle form a Möbius band. Its single edge is where the two angles meet.
Every chord of the squares and pronic mirrors lands on one rung of the band: the reflection across the x axis.
Euler's chords scatter over the whole band, because the direction of its mirror swings from one turn to the next.
So cancellation and anti-cancellation trade places. The curves that never hold a prime are the best mirrors for pairs of primes, and a mirror's own small factors predict how good it is.

chapters.title: The sieve machine
chapters.subtitle: Fermat's walk through rings of residues

lines.text: To factor a number n, Fermat looked for a square, a squared, that is n more than another square, b squared. Then n is a minus b times a plus b. The search starts at the first a whose square passes n.

Most a can be ruled out without taking a square root. Each ring is one modulus, from three to nineteen. Its gold holes are the residues of a where a squared minus n can still be a square; the dark ones are ruled out.
Step a by one, and every ring turns by one hole. Light from the centre runs out through the window until a closed ring stops it.
At a equals forty-nine every ring is open, and forty-nine squared minus fifteen hundred and one is nine hundred, thirty squared. So fifteen hundred and one is nineteen times seventy-nine.
One ring never closed. The ring for nineteen is gold all the way round, because nineteen divides fifteen hundred and one. For a prime ring, no dark holes means the prime is a factor.

For fifty thousand three hundred and ninety-nine, the light first escapes at a equals three hundred, the seventy-sixth candidate. Three hundred squared minus fifty thousand three hundred and ninety-nine is a hundred and ninety-nine squared, so it is a hundred and one times four hundred and ninety-nine.
Here is the record: one row per candidate, one column per ring. Only one row passes every column, and it is the answer.

D. H. Lehmer built sieves like this, first from bicycle chains, then in 1932 from gears and a photocell. They are fast when the two factors are close together. When the factors are far apart, a has to climb a long way, and the rings only shorten the climb by a constant factor.

chapters.title: Twisted tori
chapters.subtitle: a knot of residues and the umbilic torus

lines.text: Here is a different twist. Put each number n a seventh of a turn further around a torus, and a fifth of a turn further around its tube. The numbers wind a torus knot through thirty-five beads.
Every prime except five and seven lands on one of twenty-four beads. The other eleven beads lie on two red circles, the multiples of five on one and the multiples of seven on the other.
Euler's line visits only twelve of the twenty-four and never touches a red circle: its discriminant, minus a hundred and sixty-three, has no square root modulo five or seven.
This torus is the sieve machine with two rings: turning both by one notch steps along the knot. A torus of residues sorts the numbers; it cannot find a prime the residues have not already allowed.

Now wind the spiral itself around a torus, one lap per turn. This is Ferguson's umbilic torus. Its tube is a three-cornered deltoid that twists a third of a turn every lap, so its single edge runs around three times before it closes.
Cut at the squares ray, every cross-section has three positions, and turn k always lands in position k mod three. The turns sort into three stacks.
Then each curve meets three on whole stacks. k squared plus k plus one is a multiple of three on every turn of one stack, and all its primes sit on the other two.

k squared plus k plus three is the reverse: two stacks cancelled, and all eight of its primes on the third. A curve whose constant is two more than a multiple of three, like Euler's, is never cancelled by three at all.
Without the twist, every turn lies on the same face, and the cancelled values mix with the primes.

A half twist of a flat strip is a Möbius band, which sorts the turns by parity, and a tube with q corners sorts them mod q. The twisted shapes make residues visible, and that is all they do: the sorting is the residue lattice, drawn on a surface.
